reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Defined by sustained or intermittent involuntary muscle contractions producing abnormal, often twisting or patterned postures and repetitive movements
Movements are typically patterned and directional, may be action-specific (such as writer's cramp), and often worsen with fatigue or stress and lessen with rest or sleep
A characteristic feature is the sensory trick (geste antagoniste), where a light touch to the affected region temporarily reduces the dystonic posture
Classified by body distribution (focal, segmental, multifocal, hemidystonia, or generalised) and by age of onset and cause
Focal forms such as cervical dystonia (torticollis), blepharospasm, and laryngeal dystonia are the most common adult presentations
Botulinum toxin injection is a mainstay for focal and segmental dystonia, while oral agents and deep brain stimulation are options for more widespread disease
Young-onset generalised dystonia may be genetic (for example DYT1) and warrants a therapeutic trial of levodopa to exclude dopa-responsive dystonia
Secondary dystonia should be considered when there are additional neurological signs, a fixed posture, or hemidystonia pointing to a structural lesion
reference.pathophysiology: Dystonia arises from dysfunction of motor networks centred on the basal ganglia and their connections with the cerebellum, thalamus, and cortex, leading to loss of inhibition, abnormal sensorimotor integration, and maladaptive plasticity. Co-contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles with overflow to adjacent muscles produces the abnormal postures. Causes range from inherited (isolated or combined genetic forms) and idiopathic disease to acquired lesions, drugs, and neurodegenerative or metabolic disorders.
additionalDifferentials: Spasticity and other causes of abnormal posturing
Parkinson disease and atypical parkinsonism with dystonic features
Stiff person syndrome and orthopaedic causes of fixed posture
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain, particularly for hemidystonia or when a secondary structural cause is suspected
A trial of levodopa in young-onset generalised dystonia to identify dopa-responsive dystonia
Serum copper and ceruloplasmin and slit-lamp examination to exclude Wilson disease in younger patients
Genetic testing for hereditary dystonias where indicated
Medication review for dopamine-blocking and other offending drugs
redFlags: Acute severe dystonic reaction, especially involving the larynx or airway, requiring urgent treatment
Hemidystonia or fixed dystonia with other focal signs suggesting a structural lesion needing imaging
Young onset with hepatic or psychiatric features suggesting Wilson disease
Status dystonicus with continuous severe spasms causing rhabdomyolysis or respiratory compromise
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies with cause and distribution. Focal dystonias are usually chronic but not life-threatening and often respond well to botulinum toxin. Dopa-responsive dystonia can improve dramatically with treatment. Young-onset genetic generalised dystonia tends to spread and be more disabling, though deep brain stimulation can help selected patients.
pitfalls: Failing to trial levodopa in young-onset dystonia and missing highly treatable dopa-responsive dystonia
Overlooking Wilson disease, a treatable cause, in a young patient
Not recognising drug-induced dystonia and continuing the offending dopamine-blocking agent
Mislabelling dystonia as functional, or vice versa, without adequate assessment
management: Use botulinum toxin injection into overactive muscles as the mainstay for focal and segmental dystonia such as cervical dystonia, blepharospasm and laryngeal dystonia
Trial levodopa in young-onset generalised dystonia to identify and treat dopa-responsive dystonia
Offer oral centrally acting agents such as anticholinergics, baclofen and benzodiazepines for generalised or more widespread disease
Consider deep brain stimulation of the globus pallidus for refractory, disabling generalised or segmental dystonia
Identify and withdraw offending dopamine-blocking drugs and treat secondary causes such as Wilson disease
Provide physiotherapy and occupational therapy, and teach use of the sensory trick for symptomatic relief
Offer genetic testing and counselling in hereditary forms, with multidisciplinary neurology referral
Manage status dystonicus urgently with supportive care, sedation and intensive-care escalation
